text: In this activity, we are going to perform cluster analysis using Spark.
We will start this activity by scaling all features so that each feature is zero normalized,
then we will create an elbow plot to determine the right value for k, which is the number of
clusters to use in the k-means algorithm, then we will perform cluster analysis on a dataset using
k-means and finally we will create parallel coordinates plots to analyze the cluster centers.
As you already know the first thing that we have to do is to start our Jupyter Coursera container
and to do this we open Docker Desktop and click on the start button. Once the container is running
we click on this link that will open our browser and transfer us to JupyterLab
and here we open the big data for folder and the clustering notebook that is the
notebook for this activity.
With the notebook open we are going to proceed to load our data. So first we
are going to import all the necessary libraries and classes that we need for
this activity and once we do this we proceed to load the minor weather CSV
file as we have done before keeping the header true and inferring the schema.
Let's do some data pre-processing. We will start by counting the number of observations in our
data frame and we notice that we have almost 1.6 million observations which is just a lot for the
purposes of this activity. So instead of working with the full data frame we're going to filter
and create a filtered data frame only keeping one tenth of the original data frame. So we run this
cell and now we only have almost 160,000 observations. We take a quick look at the
descriptive statistics of this data frame and something that you need to know is that this
data was collected during a period of drought in the city of San Diego so it's very likely that
the variables related to rain do not offer much information. We can verify this by counting the
number of rows that have a value of zero for both rain accumulation and rain duration, and we see
that it's almost all of the observations in our filtered data frame. So what we're going to do is
that we're going to create a new data frame, our working data frame, and we're going to drop the
rain variables along with the timestamp. Finally we are going to drop every single row that might
contain a missing value and we're going to see how many rows we lose in this process
and we only lost 46 rows after dropping the missing values.
With our subset ready we will proceed to scale our features so first we take again a quick look
to the columns of our working data frame and instead of using all of the columns what we
will do is that we will create a list with the features that we actually plan to use
and then we will use again the vector assembler class to create a column vector and add this
column vector to our working data frame in a new data frame called assembler. Then we will create
a scalar object to scale these features keeping the mean as 0 and the standard deviation as 1.
And finally we add this to our assembled data frame.
After scaling our data we will proceed to create an elbow plot so first we select the features
and the row id we only keep one third of the scale data and we create a new elbow set.
Then we will define a range of clusters from 2 to 30 or values for k and we will start this
function that will perform a training on the elbow set and calculate the within
cluster sum of square error so we can make our plot and decide which is the best value for k.
So we wait for this training to be completed and after completing our training for a cluster size
of 30 we can use the list of values that we just stored and make the plot to make a decision on
the right value of k. So we run this cell and now we have our plot ready to be analyzed. If we take
a look at this plot we will see that on the y axis we will have the sum of square errors
and on the x-axis we have the different values for k or clusters and the idea of
this plot is to choose a value of k that allows us to create a model that is not
overfitting and we can notice that yellow is pretty much somewhere in
between a cluster value of 10 or 15 so we are going to choose 12 in this case
as the value for k to train our model.
With our value for k selected we are going to select the features that we
will use to cluster and we're going to persist this data in memory so we can
get faster access to it. So we run this and now we're going to define the k-means
algorithm with a value of k of 12, the following seed, and we're going to fit
the model using the data that we persisted. And finally we will apply
this model to this to the same data. So we run this cell, we wait for a few seconds,
and our clusters should be defined. We run this to take a look at the cluster centers,
and these are the centers of the 12 clusters that we defined.
This is not very readable, so we will proceed to plot them to get a better view of them.
We will proceed to create parallel plots of our clusters.
So the first cell that we run creates a data frame with the cluster center coordinates
and the cluster label.
As a first example, let's show clusters for dry days, this means days with a relative
humidity below 0.5.
We can see that all of the clusters in this plot have a relative humidity below 0 and
more specifically below 0.5, but their values for other features are very different.
Now take a look at cluster number 5.
This cluster has lower than average wind direction.
If we recall that these are values capturing degrees, this will mean that these are samples
with wind coming from the north and the northeast.
This is also a cluster in which samples have higher than average wind speed.
These are all patterns of something that we know as Santana winds, which are very common
in California and increase the risk of wildfires.
Now we will show clusters with high air temperature.
As we see, all of these clusters have a high value for air temperature, but they have very
different values in other features. Now we will represent clusters for cool days.
This means clusters with high relative humidity and low air temperature.
Notice that in cluster number 2 we also have high values for wind speed, which
suggests that this might be a cluster of samples for rainy and stormy days. To
conclude, we will return a plot using the index, in this case cluster number 2.
This is the cluster number 2 that we have previously seen, and this is how we conclude this activity.
